description: From an L-sit, raise your legs toward the ceiling and measure the angle. That angle is a pure readout of hip leverage: compression strength that no crunch has ever measured. Take the V-sit test and learn the truth about the front of your hips.

scenes.narration: Sit on the floor with your legs straight out in front of you, hands planted beside your hips. Press down through straight arms and lift your whole body, legs together, into an L-sit: body vertical, legs horizontal, one clean letter L. If the full L is not there yet, do the test on the edge of a chair or between two sturdy chairs, where the lift is cheaper. Now, keeping your legs straight and together, raise them slowly from horizontal toward the ceiling, folding at the hips like a closing jackknife, and stop at the highest angle you can hold for three seconds without bending your knees or leaning your chest back. Film it from the side, or have someone read the angle: horizontal is zero, straight up is ninety. That angle is your number. Keep it somewhere safe. At the end I will tell you what it reveals about the most undertrained lever in your whole body.

beats.text: IT TELLS US WHERE TO TRAIN

scenes.label: STRAIGHT UP IS THE LINE
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Ninety degrees, legs pointing at the ceiling from a pressed-up L, is the full V-sit, the complete fold. Under twenty degrees, your compression strength is unbuilt, which is the normal human condition and says nothing bad about you; almost nobody trains this lever on purpose. Over sixty degrees, your hip leverage is elite territory, the range gymnasts live in. Here is the truth this angle tells. Every ab exercise you know trains your trunk bending or resisting. The V-sit trains something else entirely: your hip flexors pulling your legs up against gravity while your trunk stays tall, a lever that gets heavier with every degree. Your angle is the exact point where your hip leverage can no longer pay the rising bill, and that point, measured honestly, is one of the most useful numbers in core training, because it tells us precisely where to train.
scenes.sub: under 20: compression is unbuilt - over 60: elite hip leverage

lines: The psoas links spine to legs.
beats.title: THE DEEPEST MUSCLE

scenes.narration: Look inside the hip, because this lever is misunderstood by almost everyone. The muscle that raises your leg is not one muscle but a team led by the iliopsoas, the deepest muscle in your body, running from your spine, through your pelvis, to the top of your thigh. It is the only muscle that connects your spine to your legs, and in the V-sit it works at a brutal disadvantage: as your legs rise, the lever arm of your legs against the hip grows, while the psoas pulls at an angle that gets worse, not better. Assisting it are the front thigh muscles, which must also keep your knees straight while the hip folds, two jobs at once. This is hip leverage: enormous load, poor angles, deep muscles. It is also why the V-sit cannot be cheated with momentum for long. Swing buys five degrees. The other eighty-five are paid in compression strength, degree by degree.

The science of compression starts with a confession: hip flexors have a public relations problem. They are blamed for tightness, back pain and bad posture, usually by people who then train everything except them. The research picture is more honest. Strong, well-trained hip flexors are essential for sprinting, kicking, climbing and every folded skill in gymnastics, and weakness in this chain is a genuine performance ceiling. What the V-sit adds to the science is measurement. Compression strength is nearly impossible to grade with ordinary exercises, because crunches and leg raises let momentum and trunk bending do the work. The pressed L removes those cheats: your arms fix your trunk, the floor removes the swing, and the angle becomes a clean dial of hip leverage. There is also a flexibility partner in this test. If your hamstrings are short, they will stop the fold before your strength does, and the angle will under-report you. We will separate those two limits in the deep dive, because they need different training.

The leg swing is where we separate the two limits. Stand tall, hold a wall, and swing one leg forward and up, keeping it straight, letting momentum carry it as high as it goes. That height is your hamstring length talking; passive, unloaded, free. Compare it with your V-sit angle, where the same leg rises under its own power. The gap between the swing's height and the sit's angle is your compression deficit, the exact size of the strength you do not yet own. A small gap means strength training will move your number fast. A huge gap means the same. The swing also warms the hip for compression work better than any static stretch, because it teaches the joint its range at speed before we ask it to hold range under load.

Your advantage in the fold is, predictably by now, mass. The lever being raised is your legs, and the bill is their weight times their length. Lighter legs are a cheaper raise at every degree, which means your hip flexors can train compression more often, with more total reps, before fatigue turns practice into swinging. The heavy athlete's V-sit work is rationed by the very mass he is trying to lift. Yours is rationed by your calendar. And there is a hidden second advantage: the V-sit's support position, pressing your body up on straight arms, is itself cheaper at your weight, so your shoulders and triceps can hold the platform while the hips do the learning. Gymnastics is an ecosystem of light bodies doing folded things. You were issued the body. This test is one of the places it cashes in.

Now we fold together. Three rounds: from your L, raise the legs as high as you honestly can, lower slowly, and repeat for the work block. Bent knees are allowed today if straight ones fold you in half.

beats.text: CLOSE THE GAP FROM BOTH ENDS

scenes.narration: Your week. Three compression sessions, each starting with leg swings to open the range at speed. The main work is raises like our block, done at the edge of your honest angle, plus seated compression lifts: sitting tall, hands beside your hips, lift one straight leg off the floor and hold five seconds, alternating. Mistake one: leaning the chest back to raise the legs. That trades hip angle for trunk angle and the dial reads a lie; stay tall and accept the smaller honest number. Mistake two: bending the knees to climb higher. A bent knee shortens the lever and the bill; the test prices straight legs only. Mistake three: ignoring the hamstrings. If your swing test showed a length limit, ten minutes of gentle forward folds across the week will raise your ceiling while strength raises your floor. Train both ends of the gap and the gap closes from both sides, which is the fastest honest math in this episode.

So, your angle. Under twenty degrees: compression is unbuilt, the most normal result in this entire season, and the fastest to improve in the first month. Twenty to forty-five: your hip leverage is real and rising; the raises will feel stronger weekly. Over forty-five: you own compression most trained men have never built, and skills like the press and the manna progression stop being jokes. Over sixty: elite hip leverage, full stop. Put your degrees in the comments, just the number, and retest in thirty days from the same support, filmed from the same side. Angles do not flatter and they do not forget. Yours is about to start climbing, and we will measure every degree of it.

Thirty days from now, same support, legs straight, fold and film it. Bring me a bigger angle and we will aim it at the ceiling together. Subscribe, and keep your number safe until then. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: Your V-Sit Angle Reveals the Truth About Your hip leverage
